# The Aldern Valley

The Aldern is a river of moderate length that rises among the moorland heights of the Carrow Fells and runs for roughly forty miles south and east before it joins the broader Wenne below the market town of Selby Cross. Along its course it passes through three distinct kinds of country. In its upper reaches it is a fast upland stream cut into hard rock. Through its middle section it widens into a valley of meadows, woods and small fields. In its lower course it is a slow, looping river across a flat plain of silt and gravel. The settlements, mills, roads and bridges of the valley were shaped by these differences, and their history begins with the rocks.

The oldest rocks in the Aldern basin lie at its head. The summits of the Carrow Fells, including the long whaleback of High Carrow and the steeper crag-edged mass of Gallow Pike, are built of dark grey gritstone and mudstone laid down as sediment on the floor of an ancient sea. These beds were later buried, compressed and folded by slow movements of the earth's crust until they were tilted steeply and in places stood almost on edge. The gritstone is coarse and resistant, made of sand grains and small quartz pebbles cemented tightly together. The mudstones between its beds are softer and split readily into thin flakes. Where the two alternate on the fellsides, weathering has left the gritstone standing out as low scarps and ledges, while the mudstone has worn back into gentle hollows. From a distance the upper slopes therefore look stepped or ribbed, with lines of crag running across the hillsides like the courses of a ruined wall.

Downstream of the fells the river crosses onto a younger and quite different series of rocks. A broad band of pale limestone forms the country around the middle valley. It was laid down in a warm, shallow sea that once lapped against the older land of the Carrow highlands, and it is made largely of the crushed shells and skeletons of small marine creatures, with occasional beds packed with whole fossils of shellfish and the stems of sea lilies. The limestone is jointed into rough blocks by vertical cracks and horizontal bedding planes, and rainwater, which is faintly acidic, has widened many of these cracks as it seeps downward. On the open tops above the middle valley the rock surface is broken into clints and grikes, flat slabs divided by deep narrow fissures in which ferns and small woodland plants find shelter from wind and grazing animals. Beneath the surface the water has dissolved passages and caves, and several streams that rise on the fells sink into the limestone at swallow holes and run underground for a mile or more before reappearing as springs on the valley sides.

Above the limestone, and forming the lower slopes of the middle valley and the ridges that enclose it, lies a sequence of sandstones, shales and thin coal seams. These rocks were formed in swamps and river deltas that spread across the region after the limestone sea withdrew. The sandstones are buff or reddish brown, softer than the gritstone of the fells but strong enough for building, and they break into regular blocks that can be dressed into square stones. The shales are grey and crumbly, and where they are exposed in stream banks they slump easily. The coal seams are mostly thin and of poor quality in the Aldern basin, but here and there they outcrop on the hillsides as black streaks in the soil.

The lower valley rests on the youngest solid rocks of the basin, a series of soft red mudstones and sandstones laid down in a hot, dry age when much of the land was desert. These red beds weather quickly into fine soil and seldom form crags. Over most of the lower valley they are hidden beneath later deposits, and they appear only in the sides of deep lanes and in the cliffs that the river has cut into its outer bends, where they show as bright brick-red faces streaked with paler bands of sand.

The present form of the valley owes much to the ice ages. During the colder periods glaciers spread down from the Carrow Fells and filled the upper part of the basin. The ice moved slowly downhill under its own weight, dragging rock fragments along its base, and it scraped and deepened the existing stream valley into a broad trough with steep sides and a flatter floor. At the head of the Aldern, beneath the eastern face of Gallow Pike, a small glacier carved a deep armchair-shaped hollow known as Carrow Comb. When the ice melted, a small dark tarn was left in the bottom of the hollow, held in by a low ridge of boulders and gravel that the glacier had pushed up at its snout. The tarn, called Comb Water, is the highest standing water in the valley, and the river's first clear channel runs out of it through a gap in the boulder ridge.

Lower down, the glaciers left their burden of ground-up rock spread across the valley floor and lower slopes as a thick, stiff clay studded with stones of every size. This boulder clay covers much of the middle valley and gives its fields their heavy, slow-draining soils. In places the ice shaped the clay into smooth oval mounds, all aligned in the direction of the ice movement, so that the land between the villages of Hartshaw and Ewen Bridge has a rolling, egg-box appearance. Large boulders of gritstone carried down from the fells lie scattered across the limestone country, some of them perched on small pedestals of limestone where the surrounding rock has dissolved away around them since the ice retreated.

As the climate warmed and the ice wasted away, great quantities of meltwater poured down the valley. These floods carried sand and gravel far beyond the ice margin and laid them down across the lower valley in broad, flat spreads. Later, as the volume of water fell and the river settled into a narrower course, it cut down into these deposits and left parts of them standing as terraces along the valley sides. Two main terraces can be traced through much of the lower valley. The higher of them lies some way above the modern flood level and forms a dry, level bench of well-drained gravel; the lower one sits closer to the river and is occasionally reached by the highest floods. Below them both lies the modern floodplain, a ribbon of fine silt and clay laid down by the river each time it overflows its banks.

At one point the retreating ice paused long enough to block the valley near the present village of Lowther Ings, and a temporary lake formed behind it. Fine mud settled on the lake floor in thin layers, one pair of light and dark bands for each summer and winter. When the ice barrier finally gave way the lake drained, but its bed remained as a broad flat basin floored with pale, sticky clay. This basin later became the great water meadows of the Ings, and its clay was dug for bricks and tiles in a later age.

The river that runs through this landscape changes its character from source to mouth. Below Comb Water the young Aldern is a narrow torrent, falling steeply over ledges of gritstone in a series of small cascades. Its bed is a jumble of rounded boulders, and its water is clear but stained the colour of weak tea by peat washed from the moorland above. At Thrang Force, a little more than four miles below the tarn, the river drops over a lip of hard gritstone into a deep plunge pool, having cut a narrow gorge back into the rock behind the fall over thousands of years. The sound of the fall can be heard across the open fell in wet weather, when the river rises quickly after rain.

On reaching the limestone the river loses part of its flow. In dry summers much of the water slips away into fissures in its bed, and for a stretch of about two miles above the village of Skelder the channel may run almost dry, leaving a bare pavement of white stones. The water does not disappear but travels through hidden passages and returns to the surface at a group of strong springs below the village, where it rises cold and clear and remarkably constant in volume through the year. The springs at Skelder, known together as the Boilings, are the most reliable source of water in the valley, and the river below them rarely shrinks however dry the season.

Through the middle valley the river winds across a floodplain of moderate width between wooded slopes. Its bed here is of gravel and cobbles, and it divides into riffles, where shallow water runs quickly over stones, and pools, where it deepens and slows. During floods it shifts its gravel bars and sometimes cuts new channels across the inside of its bends. In the lower valley the gradient becomes very gentle, and the river swings in broad meanders across its plain. It undercuts the outer bank of each bend, where the current is strongest, and builds up beaches of sand and silt on the inner bank, where the current slackens. Over time the bends migrate slowly downstream and outward. When two bends grow close enough together the river breaks through the narrow neck of land between them and abandons the loop, which becomes a still, curved pool or oxbow. Several such pools lie on the plain near Selby Cross, gradually filling with reeds and silt.

The vegetation of the valley after the ice ages developed in stages as the climate warmed. The first plants to colonise the raw glacial ground were low mosses, sedges, grasses and creeping dwarf shrubs, much like those that grow on high mountain tops today. These were followed by birch and pine, and then, as the warmth increased, by hazel, oak, elm, lime and alder. At its greatest extent the woodland covered almost the whole valley except for the highest fell tops, the wettest bogs and the open water. The lower slopes and the valley floor carried a dense, mixed forest of oak and lime with elm on the richer soils and hazel in the understorey. Alder and willow crowded along the riverbanks and in the wet hollows of the floodplain, and it is from the alder that the river is held to take its name, the old form of the word meaning a stream fringed with alders.

On the gritstone fells a different pattern developed. The heavy rainfall of the uplands washed nutrients out of the thin, acidic soils, and as the woods on the high ground thinned, a layer of peat began to form. Peat builds up where the ground stays so wet that dead plant matter cannot rot completely, and on the flatter summits of the Carrow Fells it accumulated slowly, year upon year, until it formed a blanket several feet deep across the tops. Stumps of pine and birch can still be seen in places where streams have cut through the peat to its base, showing that trees once grew where there is now only open moor. The surface of the blanket bog is covered with cotton grass, heather, bilberry and sphagnum moss, and it is broken by wet pools and by deep channels called hags where the peat has been eroded.

The limestone country of the middle valley supported its own distinctive plants. Ash woods grew on the steep scars and in the dry valleys, with an understorey of hazel, hawthorn and bird cherry and a ground layer rich in wild garlic, dog's mercury and early purple orchids. On the thin soils of the open limestone the turf was short and fine and full of small flowering herbs, among them thyme, rockrose, bird's-foot trefoil and blue moor grass. The deep fissures of the limestone pavement held hart's-tongue fern, wood sorrel and herb Robert in their damp shade.

Animal life in the early woodland included red deer, roe deer, wild cattle, wild boar, wolves, brown bears, beavers, otters and a great variety of smaller mammals and birds. Beavers dammed the side streams of the middle valley and created a chain of ponds and marshes along the lower reaches of becks such as Ewen Beck and the Skelder Sike. Salmon and sea trout ran up the river each year from the Wenne to spawn in the clean gravels of the middle and upper reaches, and brown trout and eels lived in the river throughout its length. The marshes and pools of the lower valley were the haunt of herons, bitterns, cranes and great numbers of wildfowl in winter.

The first people to enter the valley came as hunters and gatherers in the period after the ice had gone, moving with the seasons along the river and up onto the fells in pursuit of deer and other game. They camped on the dry gravel terraces of the lower valley and on knolls overlooking the river in the middle reaches, and they left behind scatters of small, finely worked flint blades and points, along with the ashes of their hearths. Flint does not occur naturally in the Aldern basin, and the pieces that these people used had been carried in from the chalk country far to the south and east. On the fells they made use of the open ground near the tree line, where game could be watched and followed, and a few of their small camps have been found on spurs above Carrow Comb and near the head of Thrang Gill, where shelter, water and wide views could be had together.

These early inhabitants made only slight changes to the woodland, though they may have used fire to clear small glades where grazing animals would gather and where hazel would grow vigorously for its nuts. Over many generations their way of life slowly gave way to another, in which people began to keep livestock, grow cereal crops and settle more permanently in one place. With that change the long transformation of the Aldern valley from wildwood to farmed land began.

# The Aldern Valley: Part 2, Waters, Woodland and the First Settlements

The Aldern rises as a cluster of seepages on the eastern flank of Carrow Fell, where rain soaking into the peat of the upper moor meets the impermeable shales beneath and is forced out sideways along the slope. These seepages gather into a series of small, tea-coloured channels that run over bare rock and through cushions of sphagnum moss before joining, at a height of a little under five hundred metres, into a single stream known locally as the Aldern Beck. For its first few kilometres the beck descends steeply through the narrow ravine cut into the gritstone escarpment, falling in a succession of short cascades and plunge pools. The largest of these, the Linn of Harrowgill, drops some nine metres over a lip of hard sandstone into a bowl worn smooth by the swirling of gravel and boulders during floods. Below the Linn the gradient eases, the ravine opens, and the beck becomes a river in its own right as it enters the broad glacial trough that forms the heart of the valley.

The behaviour of the river is governed largely by the rock and soil it passes over. On the high moor, rain runs off quickly because the peat is already saturated for most of the year, and the upper Aldern rises within hours of heavy rainfall. In a summer thunderstorm the water level at the foot of the Linn can climb by more than a metre in an afternoon and fall back almost as fast. Lower down, where the river crosses the limestone band that underlies the middle valley, part of its flow sinks into fissures in the bed. In dry summers the stretch between the hamlet of Sallow Cross and the Brindle meadows sometimes runs almost dry, the water travelling instead through underground passages and reappearing at a line of springs near Eastwick, where it wells up cold and clear at a nearly constant temperature through the year. These springs give the lower river a steadier flow than the upper reaches, and they have never been known to freeze.

Below Eastwick the Aldern meanders across the floor of the trough in wide loops, following the soft clays and sands left by the retreating ice. Here the river is constantly reshaping its course. On the outer side of each bend the current undercuts the bank, which slumps into the water in blocks of turf and soil; on the inner side gravel and silt build up into low beaches and bars, which in time are colonised by willow and sedge. Over centuries this slow sideways movement has left the valley floor patterned with abandoned channels. Some are still visible as crescent-shaped ponds or damp hollows filled with rushes; others have filled completely and can be traced only as faint curving lines where the grass grows a darker green in dry weather. The largest of these old loops, the Cutoff at Wenley, was separated from the main river during a great flood and remained an open lake for many generations before silting into a reed-bed.

Floods are a regular part of the river's life. Winter rain falling on frozen or saturated ground, or a sudden thaw of snow lying on the moor, sends a surge of water down the valley that overtops the banks and spreads across the floor of the trough. In the lower valley the floodwater may cover the meadows for several days, moving slowly and laying down a thin film of fine silt as it retreats. This regular deposition has given the meadows their deep, dark, fertile soil, free of stones and easily worked. The higher terraces along the valley sides, formed of sand and gravel laid down by meltwater at the close of the ice age, stand above the reach of all but the rarest floods. Their soils are lighter and drain freely, warming quickly in spring.

The climate of the valley is mild and damp, shaped by moist westerly winds that drop much of their rain on the fells before passing east. The upper moor is wet, windy and frequently shrouded in cloud, and snow can lie there well into spring. The lower valley, sheltered by the surrounding hills, is noticeably drier and warmer, and its growing season begins several weeks earlier than on the moor. On still winter nights, cold air drains down the side valleys and collects on the valley floor, so that frost and fog are common in the meadows while the slopes above remain clear. The villages of the Aldern have, for this reason, almost all grown up on the terraces and lower slopes rather than on the flat ground nearest the river.

Before people cleared the land, the valley was almost entirely wooded below the moorland edge. On the upper slopes, where soils were thin and acidic, birch and rowan grew among scattered pines, with an understorey of heather, bilberry and bracken. On the deeper soils of the middle slopes the forest was dominated by oak, with hazel forming a dense shrub layer beneath. Hazel thrives in the half-light under oak and produces abundant nuts in autumn, and it remained one of the most common plants of the valley long after much of the oak had gone. Ash and wych elm grew on the limestone, where the soil was richer and less acidic, and their woods were carpeted in spring with wild garlic, bluebells and dog's mercury.

The wettest ground along the river supported a different woodland altogether. Here alder, from which the river is said to take its name, formed dense stands on the waterlogged silts, its roots able to survive in soil that is flooded for much of the year. Alder carries nodules on its roots in which bacteria fix nitrogen from the air, allowing the tree to grow on soils that would starve most others. Its leaves, falling into the river in autumn, decay quickly and enrich the water. Willow and bird cherry grew among the alders, and the ground beneath was a tangle of tussock sedge, marsh marigold, meadowsweet and yellow flag. In the oldest abandoned channels, where water stood all year, these alder woods graded into open fen with reed and bulrush.

The animals of this forested valley included red and roe deer, wild boar, badger, fox, pine marten and wildcat, with wolves ranging through the woods and onto the moor. Beavers lived along the slower reaches of the lower river, felling willow and alder and building dams across the side channels. Their dams held back water in a chain of shallow ponds, spreading the river across the valley floor and creating patches of open, flooded ground among the trees. Otters hunted along the whole length of the river. The Aldern itself held brown trout in its upper reaches and salmon and sea trout, which ran up from the sea each autumn to spawn in the clean gravels below the Linn. The spawning fish cut shallow hollows in the gravel, called redds, in which the eggs were laid and covered over, and the young fish spent one or more years in the river before going down to the sea. Eels were abundant in the lower river and in the ponds and channels of the valley floor.

The first people to live in the valley came as hunters and gatherers, moving through it with the seasons. They camped on the dry gravel terraces close to the river, where they could fish, gather hazelnuts and hunt deer and boar in the surrounding woods. Their camps were small and temporary, consisting of shelters of poles covered with hides or bark, built around a hearth. They used tools of flint and chert, the flint carried in from the coast and the chert gathered from beds within the limestone of the middle valley. The edges of these tools were worked into small blades and points that were set in wooden or bone handles to make arrows, knives and scrapers. In summer, groups moved up onto the high ground, following the deer to the open moorland edge, and they set small fires there to keep clearings open, encouraging fresh grass and browse that drew the animals in.

Farming reached the Aldern much later, bringing with it a more lasting pattern of settlement. The early farmers cleared patches of woodland on the light, well-drained soils of the terraces and lower slopes, cutting and burning the trees and planting wheat and barley among the stumps. They kept cattle, sheep, goats and pigs, the pigs foraging in the oakwoods for acorns and the cattle grazing in the clearings and along the river. Fields were small and roughly square, bounded by banks of earth and stone gathered as the ground was cleared. These farmers built round houses of timber and wattle, plastered with daub made from clay and straw and roofed with thatch, each with a central hearth whose smoke rose through the roof. A few households clustered together formed a settlement, and some of these were surrounded by a bank and ditch with a timber fence along the top, to keep in livestock and keep out wild animals.

On the moor above the valley, these early communities raised stone monuments. A ring of standing stones, known as the Carrow Maidens, stands on a level shelf of ground below the summit of Carrow Fell, looking down the length of the valley. The stones are slabs of local gritstone, the tallest standing about twice the height of a person, set upright in a circle some thirty metres across. Nearby, a number of low cairns of heaped stone mark burials, and lines of smaller stones run across the moor between them. At the time these were built, the moor was less wet than it later became, and its lighter soils carried a mixture of open grassland and scattered woodland that was grazed and in places cultivated.

Over the following centuries the clearing of the woods continued, and the face of the valley slowly changed. As more trees were removed from the high ground, the soils there were exposed to heavy rain and began to lose their nutrients, which were washed downward out of reach of plant roots. The ground became more acidic and waterlogged, and peat began to accumulate on the flatter parts of the moor, spreading over old fields and burying the bases of some of the standing stones. The upper slopes, once wooded, became the open heather moor that has covered them ever since. Soil washed from the cleared slopes was carried down by the river and deposited on the valley floor, adding to the layers of silt in the meadows.

By the time iron came into use, the valley held a scattering of farmsteads along its whole length, together with a small hillfort on the spur of Rowan Knoll, which juts out from the northern slope above the middle valley. The fort was enclosed by a double rampart of earth and rubble faced with stone, with a deep ditch between, and its entrance was a narrow passage between the overlapping ends of the ramparts. Within the enclosure stood a number of round houses and raised granaries built on posts to keep grain dry and away from rodents. From the knoll there is a clear view both up the valley toward the fells and down toward the coastal plain. Iron was smelted in small clay furnaces from bog ore, a deposit of iron oxide that forms in wet ground where iron-rich water from the hills meets the air. The bog ore of the Aldern was gathered from the marshy hollows of the valley floor, roasted, and smelted with charcoal made from the coppiced hazel and oak of the valley woods.

Coppicing became one of the most important ways of managing the woodland. Hazel, oak, ash and alder, when cut close to the ground, send up a cluster of new shoots from the stump, which grow straight and fast. Cut again after a number of years, these provide poles for building, fencing and wattle, as well as fuel and charcoal. A coppiced stump, called a stool, can be cut again and again over many generations, and some of the oldest stools in the Aldern woods have spread into broad rings of stems around a long-rotted centre. The woods were divided into sections, each cut in turn, so that at any time the valley held patches of woodland at every stage of regrowth, from freshly cut ground bright with spring flowers to dense thickets of tall poles.

As the farms multiplied, a network of tracks grew up to connect them. The principal route ran along the northern terraces, keeping above the floodwaters, from the coastal plain to the foot of the escarpment, and from there climbed by a steep zigzag onto the moor and over the watershed into the neighbouring valley. Lesser tracks branched down to the river at points where it could be forded. The most used of these crossings lay at Eastwick, where the spring-fed river spread across a broad bed of firm gravel and could be waded for most of the year, and at Sallow Cross, where in summer the sinking of the water into the limestone left the bed almost bare. At these fords, flat stones were laid in the riverbed to give firmer footing, and in later times rows of large stepping stones were set across the channel for those on foot.

It was around these crossings, and around the springs and dry terraces that offered both good land and shelter from the river, that the first lasting villages of the Aldern began to take shape. Farmsteads that had once stood apart drew closer together, their fields merging into larger shared areas of arable on the terraces, with meadow on the flood-enriched ground below and rough grazing on the slopes and moor above. Eastwick, Sallow Cross, Wenley and the upland settlement of Harrowgill, below the Linn, each grew up in this way, with a cluster of dwellings on rising ground, ploughland around them, and the river close at hand. In this form, each fixed to its patch of terrace and its share of meadow and moor, the villages of the valley would grow through the centuries that followed, as people turned increasingly to the river itself as a source of power.

# The Aldern Valley: Mills, Bridges and the Working River

By the close of the thirteenth century the villages of the Aldern had settled into the places they would keep for the next five hundred years. Hollin Cross stood on its gravel terrace above the upper gorge, Wethercombe spread along the spring line at the foot of the western scarp, and Saltry, the largest of the valley settlements, sat where the river slackened and widened before entering the clay vale. Between and around them the river itself began to change. It was no longer only a boundary, a fishing water and a source of flood. It became a source of power, and over the following centuries the Aldern was harnessed, divided, embanked and crossed until much of its course was as much a made thing as a natural one.

The first mills on the Aldern were small undershot wheels set directly into the current. They stood at points where the channel narrowed between rock outcrops, so that the water ran fast without the need for much construction. The earliest of them, below Hollin Cross, was a timber building on a stone footing, with a wheel of oak paddles turning in a slot cut partly into the limestone of the riverbed. The wheel drove a single pair of stones through a horizontal shaft and a cog-and-rung gear, grinding barley and oats for the upland farms. Such mills turned slowly and stopped altogether in dry summers, when the upper river shrank to a chain of pools linked by a trickle over the bedrock. In winter they were at the mercy of floods that carried trees and ice down the gorge, and the Hollin Cross mill was rebuilt at least three times on the same footing before the end of the fourteenth century.

Lower in the valley the gradient was gentler and the river too broad and slow to turn a wheel unaided. Here the millwrights built weirs. A weir on the Aldern was at first a line of driven timber stakes set across the channel at a slant, the gaps packed with brushwood, stones and clay. Behind it the water rose into a millpond that stretched upstream for some distance, drowning the shallows and turning a stretch of braided gravel channels into a single still reach. From the side of the pond a leat, a narrow artificial channel, carried water along the valley side at a slightly lower gradient than the river, so that by the time it reached the mill it stood several feet above the natural bed. This difference in height, the head, was what drove the wheel. Water passing through the mill fell back into the river by a tailrace, rejoining the main channel some way downstream.

The Saltry mill, built on this pattern, became the principal corn mill of the lower valley. Its leat left the river above the village, ran behind the churchyard and the backs of the street houses, and passed beneath the road in a stone culvert before reaching the mill building at the eastern edge of the settlement. The mill held two pairs of stones, one of local gritstone quarried from the eastern hills for coarse grinding and one of imported burr stone for finer flour. Its breastshot wheel received water at about the height of its axle, so that the weight of the water in the buckets as well as its movement turned the wheel. This was more efficient than the undershot wheels of the upper valley and allowed the Saltry mill to work through all but the driest weeks of the year.

The weirs had effects well beyond the mills. Each one held back sediment as well as water, and the ponds behind them slowly filled with silt and sand washed down from the ploughed slopes above. Within a few generations the reach above the Saltry weir had become shallow and marshy at its edges, with beds of reed and sedge spreading from the banks. Eels gathered in the slack water and in the leats, and eel traps of woven willow became a fixture of every mill. Fish that had once moved freely up the river to spawn on the gravels below Hollin Cross found their way barred, and the runs of sea trout that had come up the Aldern in autumn dwindled through the later medieval centuries. The river below each weir, robbed of its sediment, cut down into its bed, so that the channel became deeper and the banks steeper downstream of the mills than above them.

The floodplain itself changed in response. Meadows along the lower Aldern had always been wet in winter, but the raised water levels behind the weirs kept them wet for longer. The farmers of Saltry and Wethercombe turned this to use. From the sixteenth century onward they cut networks of shallow channels across the meadows, fed by sluices from the river or the leats. In late winter they let water flow thinly over the grass, a practice known locally as floating. The moving water kept frost from the ground and carried a fine film of silt onto the turf, so that the grass began to grow several weeks earlier than on unwatered land. The meadows were then drained, grazed by ewes and lambs in spring, and closed for hay in summer. The pattern of ridges and channels made by this work still shows across the lower floodplain as low parallel banks in the turf, most clearly when the grass is short or when floodwater lies in the old furrows.

Mills multiplied along the Aldern through the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Fulling mills appeared on the middle river, where cloth woven in the cottages of Wethercombe and the scarp-foot hamlets was brought to be cleansed and thickened. A fulling mill used its wheel to lift heavy wooden hammers, known as stocks, which fell repeatedly on the wet cloth lying in a trough with water and fuller's earth. The pounding matted the woollen fibres together, shrinking and strengthening the cloth. After fulling the cloth was stretched on tenter frames in fields beside the mill to dry, and the meadows below Wethercombe were for a time lined with rows of these frames, each length of cloth held taut by hooks along its edges. Downstream of the fulling mills the river ran grey and soapy, and the fuller's earth, a pale clay dug from a pit on the eastern hills, settled in the pools.

On the tributary streams that came down from the western scarp, smaller mills were built for other purposes. The Kell Brook, which falls steeply through a wooded combe above Wethercombe, carried a string of three mills within the space of a mile, each taking its water from the tailrace of the one above. The highest was a bark mill, crushing oak bark for the tanneries of Saltry. The middle mill ground flint and bone for the potteries and for fertiliser. The lowest was a small paper mill, which pulped linen rags in water and laid the pulp in thin sheets on wire moulds. The steep fall of the brook allowed these mills to use overshot wheels, in which water was carried by a wooden trough to the top of the wheel and dropped into the buckets, turning the wheel by weight alone. Overshot wheels needed far less water than undershot ones, which suited the small and flashy streams of the scarp.

Crossing the Aldern had always been a matter of fords. The river in its natural state was wide and shallow over much of its lower course, and there were several places where gravel bars ran nearly across the channel. The main ford at Saltry lay a little upstream of the later bridge, on a bar of coarse gravel that carried the road from the clay vale up into the valley. Carts crossed here at low water; at high water travellers waited, sometimes for days. Footbridges of timber planks laid on trestles served those on foot in the villages, but they were swept away in most floods and had to be replaced every few years.

The construction of the weirs made fords more difficult, since the raised water drowned the gravel bars and deepened the channels below. The first permanent bridge over the Aldern was built at Saltry in the late fifteenth century. It was a stone bridge of four arches, built of the same limestone as the church, each arch a pointed form springing from piers that stood on the riverbed. The piers were shaped on their upstream faces into triangular cutwaters, which split the current and turned aside floating debris. Above the cutwaters, the parapet was carried out into small triangular refuges where people on foot could step aside from passing carts. The roadway was narrow, wide enough for a single wagon, and humped over the arches so that the bridge rose noticeably from each bank to its centre.

The Saltry bridge changed the way the lower valley was used. The road through the village became a through route between the clay vale and the upland, and inns and smithies grew up along it. A small market was held on the open ground at the eastern end of the bridge, where the road widened. The bridge also changed the river. Its piers narrowed the channel, so that in flood the water backed up behind it and spread across the meadows upstream, while immediately below the bridge the current scoured deep holes in the bed. One of these pools, below the second arch, remained the deepest point on the lower Aldern for centuries and was used by the village as a washing place and, in hot summers, for bathing.

Upstream, the crossing at Hollin Cross was made by a single high arch of rubble stone, built over the narrowest point of the gorge where the river ran between limestone walls. Because the rock on either side provided natural abutments, no piers were needed in the water, and the bridge stood above the reach of all but the greatest floods. It was a packhorse bridge, with low parapets that allowed laden horses to pass without catching their panniers, and it carried a track that ran over the eastern hills to the lead workings beyond. Strings of ponies crossed it in summer carrying ore and returned with grain and salt.

Between these two crossings the middle valley remained bridgeless for longer. At Wethercombe the river was crossed by a ford and a ferry, the ferry being a flat-bottomed boat drawn across on a rope stretched between two posts. The ferry house stood on the western bank, a small stone building with a single room and a fireplace, and the ferryman kept a lantern at the window so that travellers could find the crossing after dark. A timber bridge was finally built at Wethercombe in the early eighteenth century, resting on oak piles driven into the gravel and braced with diagonal timbers. It was replaced in stone about sixty years later after the piles had been loosened by repeated floods.

The eighteenth century brought the most intensive use of the river. Corn milling expanded to serve a growing population, and several of the older mills were rebuilt in brick with larger wheels and additional pairs of stones. The Saltry mill was raised to three storeys, with a sack hoist under a projecting gable lifting grain to the top floor, from which it was fed down through the building by gravity, passing through the stones, the dressing machines and the bagging floor in turn. Its timber weir was replaced with one of dressed stone, built in a long curve across the river with a sloping face over which the water slid in a smooth sheet. A fish pass of stepped pools was built into one side, although it was too steep for most fish to climb.

At the same time, the lower Aldern was straightened and embanked for navigation. Below Saltry the river had wandered across its floodplain in broad loops, and these were cut through by new channels that shortened its course by more than a mile. The old loops, left without a through flow, silted at their ends and became still backwaters, which slowly filled with reeds and alder and turned to wet woodland. Earth banks were raised along the new channel to hold floods back from the fields, and a towpath ran along the top of the northern bank. Shallow-draught barges were hauled by horses from the vale as far as a wharf below the Saltry bridge, carrying coal, lime and timber up the valley and taking grain, cloth and tanned hides down. A pound lock beside the Saltry weir allowed barges to pass the fall, its two pairs of timber gates enclosing a chamber of stone that filled and emptied through sluices in the gates.

The navigation, the mills and the floating meadows all depended on the same water, and the river was divided among them by a growing system of sluices, hatches and side channels. In wet seasons there was water enough for all, but in dry summers the leats drew off so much of the flow that the main channel between the weir and the tailrace dwindled to a narrow stream, leaving long reaches of gravel and weed exposed. In these reaches the water warmed in the sun and grew thick with green algae, and the river below Saltry in late summer carried a distinct smell of mud and weed.

By the close of the eighteenth century the Aldern from Hollin Cross to the vale was a sequence of managed reaches, each held up by a weir and drained by a mill, joined by straightened channels and crossed by a handful of stone bridges. The valley floor was patterned with water meadows, tenter fields, osier beds and old river loops. The river still flooded in winter and still shrank in summer, but the shape of its floods and the pattern of its flow were now set as much by stone and timber as by rain and rock.

# The Aldern Valley: Natural and Settlement History (Part 4)

By the early decades of the nineteenth century the Aldern had become a working river along nearly its whole length. The water that had cut the gorge at Skelmoor and spread the gravel terraces below Sallowby now passed through a sequence of weirs, leats and wheel-pits, each of which took a share of its fall and returned it, slower and warmer, a little further downstream. The old corn mills of the medieval manors remained, but beside them and between them stood newer buildings of a different scale. The fulling mill at Holm Foot had been rebuilt in three storeys of gritstone, its single wheel replaced by a pair of breastshot wheels set side by side in a stone race. At Kettlewick a bobbin mill turned birch and alder from the valley woods into spools for the cotton towns beyond the watershed, and the sound of its lathes carried across the water meadows from dawn until the light failed.

The bobbin trade changed the woods themselves. The oak and ash coppices on the steeper valley sides had been cut for charcoal and bark for centuries, on rotations long enough to let the stools grow poles of a useful thickness. The bobbin makers wanted smaller, straighter wood, and they wanted it in quantity, so the rotation shortened and birch, which grows fast from the stump, came to dominate slopes that had once been mixed. In winter the cut poles were stacked in long ricks along the cart tracks above Kettlewick to season, and the stripped bark was carted down to the tan pits at Marrow End, where hides soaked in oak liquor in rows of timber-lined pits beside the beck. The smell of the tannery hung over the lower part of that village for most of the century, and the beck below it ran brown.

The river's power had limits that shaped where industry could settle. The Aldern carried its greatest flows in winter and early spring, when rain fell on the moorland catchment and ran quickly off the thin peat and shale. In summer the same channel could shrink to a chain of pools linked by shallow riffles, and the mills on the upper river, above the junction with Garth Beck, often stood idle for weeks in a dry August. To hold water against these lean months the millers built ponds. The largest, at Holm Foot, filled a hollow between two glacial mounds and was fed by a leat nearly a mile long, cut along the contour of the valley side so that it fell only a few feet over its whole length. From the pond a sluice released water onto the wheels as needed, and on a still evening its surface held a perfect reflection of the alder and willow that grew along its banks.

Steam came to the valley late and only in part. The coal measures lay well to the south, and every ton had to be carted over the hill road from Brackham until the railway arrived. The first steam engine in the valley was installed at the Sallowby worsted mill in the 1830s, not to replace the wheel but to support it in dry seasons, and for a generation the two ran together, the engine house with its tall square chimney standing beside the older wheel-pit. Smaller mills higher up the river never made the change. Their owners continued to depend on water, and as the century advanced and the trade concentrated in larger works with steady power, several of them closed. By the 1870s the paper mill at Ravensgill had fallen silent, its wheel removed for scrap and its roof stripped, and the building slowly settled into the bank that had been cut to hold it.

The railway reached the Aldern in 1862. The Aldern Valley line left the main route at Brackham Junction, climbed through a cutting in the boulder clay, and descended to the river at Marrow End, from where it followed the valley floor upstream as far as Kettlewick. The engineers kept to the higher terraces where they could, for the flood plain was soft and liable to inundation, but at three points the line had to cross the river. At Marrow End a viaduct of seven stone arches carried the track over both the river and the low ground beside it, its piers founded on timber piles driven down through the alluvium to the gravels beneath. At Hesketh Bridge and again below Kettlewick the crossings were made with wrought-iron girders on masonry abutments, simpler structures suited to the narrower channel. The stone for the viaduct came from a quarry opened for the purpose on the hillside above Marrow End, where the grey sandstone of the valley's middle reaches lay in thick, even beds that could be split into large blocks.

The arrival of the railway altered the pattern of the villages. Marrow End, which had been a cluster of farms, cottages and the tannery around a green, gained a station, a goods yard, a coal depot and a row of terraced houses for railway workers along the road that led up from the station to the church. The cattle fair that had been held on the green each autumn moved to a new auction mart beside the goods yard, where animals could be loaded directly into wagons. Sallowby, with its worsted mill, grew more than any other settlement; new streets of stone terraces climbed the slope behind the mill, laid out in straight rows that contrasted with the irregular plan of the older village around the market cross. Chapels of several denominations were built, along with a mechanics' institute, a school and a cooperative store with a clock above its door. Higher up the valley, where the railway did not reach, villages such as Skelmoor and Garthwaite changed far less, and their populations slowly declined as younger people left for the mill towns.

The bridges of the valley went through a corresponding transformation. Pennock Bridge, the narrow packhorse bridge of two arches that had carried the old road across the river below Holm Foot since the late medieval period, proved too narrow for the carts and wagons that now used the road. In 1848 it was widened on its downstream side, the new masonry built against the old so that from beneath the two phases could be seen clearly: the earlier arch ribs of rough-dressed stone and the later extension of smooth ashlar with a slightly different curve. At Hesketh, the timber bridge that gave the village its name had been replaced in stone in the eighteenth century, and in the 1880s its parapets were raised and its approaches regraded to ease the gradient for heavy loads. Further downstream, where the Aldern widened toward its confluence with the larger river beyond Brackham, a ferry still crossed until 1891, when an iron lattice footbridge was built on cylindrical cast-iron piers sunk into the riverbed.

The river itself responded to all of this activity. Weirs held back sediment, and the pools above them gradually filled with sand and silt until they became shallow reaches through which the current moved sluggishly. Below each weir the water, released of its load, scoured the bed and undercut the banks, and the millers and landowners protected their property with walls of dry stone, timber piling and, later, dumped rubble. Straightening was carried out in places to drain the meadows and speed the passage of floodwater; the old meanders below Sallowby were cut through in the 1850s, leaving a series of crescent-shaped hollows in the fields that filled with water in wet winters and supported sedge and yellow flag through the summer. Effluent from the tannery, the dye houses at Sallowby and the gas works at Marrow End entered the river directly, and for much of the late nineteenth century the salmon that had once run up the Aldern to spawn in the gravels below Skelmoor were absent. Trout persisted in the upper reaches and in the side becks, where the water remained clear.

The great flood of 1903 marked a turning point in the valley's relationship with its river. A storm that settled over the moors at the head of the catchment in late October brought a day and a night of continuous heavy rain onto ground already saturated, and the Aldern rose faster and higher than at any time in living memory. At Skelmoor the water filled the gorge to within a few feet of the road. At Holm Foot it overtopped the mill dam and broke through its eastern end, emptying the pond in a single surge that carried away the footbridge below and much of the leat bank. The flood plain from Sallowby to Marrow End became a single sheet of moving water. The railway embankment near Hesketh was breached, and one of the iron girder bridges was shifted on its bearings. Pennock Bridge stood, its old arches turning the flow through the widened openings, though the water rose above the springing of the arches and left a line of debris along the parapet. When the river fell, the meadows were covered with sand and gravel, and in places the channel had moved, abandoning one course and cutting another across the fields.

The repairs that followed were extensive, but several of the older works were not rebuilt. The Holm Foot dam was replaced with a lower weir and the pond was never refilled; its bed became rough grazing and, in time, a wet woodland of alder and willow. Between the wars, as the textile trade contracted, the mills of the valley closed one by one. The bobbin mill at Kettlewick shut in 1927, when plastic and metal spools began to replace wooden ones; the fulling mill at Holm Foot followed in 1931. The Sallowby worsted mill continued, powered entirely by steam and later by electricity, until 1968, when its looms were removed and the building was divided into smaller industrial units. The tannery at Marrow End closed in the 1950s, and its pits were filled with rubble and grassed over.

The railway did not outlast the mills by long. Passenger services along the Aldern Valley line ended in 1959 and goods services in 1964, and the track was lifted soon afterward. The viaduct at Marrow End remained, its seven arches standing above the river meadows, while the girder bridges at Hesketh and Kettlewick were dismantled and their abutments left on either bank. The trackbed became a path, first informally and then by designation, and it now carries walkers and cyclists along the valley floor on an even gradient, through the cutting near Brackham where the boulder clay is exposed in its sides and over the viaduct where the whole flood plain can be seen spread out below.
